content.narrative_summary: This is the title page of the guideline, providing the full title, report designation, and endorsing organizations. It lists the writing committee members with their credentials and roles, and includes publication details, approval statements by the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association committees, citation format, copyright and permissions information, and journal publication data.

Page contains administrative content including article header, author list, peer review committee members, and ACC/AHA Joint Committee membership. No clinical recommendations, tables, figures, or narrative guidance text present.

This page contains the abstract for the 2026 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia, stating the aim to retire and replace the 2018 guideline, methods involving a comprehensive literature search from October to December 2024, and the structure focusing on evaluation, management, and monitoring of individuals with dyslipidemias. Below the abstract, the table of contents lists the major sections and sub‐sections (Introduction, Definitions and Classifications, Evaluation and Diagnosis, Management, Complications of Management, Evidence Gaps and Future Directions) along with their page numbers.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 1 What Is New

rows.recommendation: In adults and children who have undergone a standard lipid profile, use of either the Martin/Hopkins equation or the Sampson/NIH equation is preferred over calculation by the Friedewald equation to estimate LDL-C.

In adults on LLT, particularly those with ASCVD, CKM syndrome, type 2 diabetes, and/or elevated TG, measurement of apoB is reasonable to guide decisions regarding further therapeutic intensification once LDL-C and/or non-HDL-C goals are achieved.
In all adults, measurement of Lp(a) concentration is recommended at least once for ASCVD risk assessment.

In individuals with dyslipidemia, the use of dietary supplements is not recommended to lower LDL-C or TG based on limited and inconsistent data and/or limited benefits in lipid-lowering and reduction in ASCVD risk.
In individuals with fasting TG ≥1000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L) referral to an RDN is recommended to create an individualized treatment plan aimed at reducing TG and the risk of pancreatitis.

In individuals with fasting TG ≥150 to 999 mg/dL (1.7–11.3 mmol/L) and features of the CKM syndrome, referral to an RDN is recommended to provide counseling on evidence-based dietary patterns that can be beneficial to improve lipoprotein levels and reduce the risk of pancreatitis.

In adults aged 30 to 79 years without ASCVD or subclinical atherosclerosis and with an LDL-C level between 70 and 189 mg/dL (1.8–4.9 mmol/L), the PREVENT-ASCVD equations should be used to estimate 10-year ASCVD risk, with categorization as having low (<3%), borderline (3% to <5%), intermediate (5% to <10%), or high (≥10%) risk.

In adults without ASCVD with a borderline 10-year ASCVD risk estimate (3% to <5%) by the PREVENT-ASCVD equations, consideration of risk enhancers is reasonable to personalize risk assessment and the potential benefit of initiating LLT as an adjunct to lifestyle management to reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults without ASCVD with a borderline 10-year ASCVD risk estimate (3% to <5%) by the PREVENT-ASCVD equations, if hsCRP is measured and is ≥2 mg/L on 2 successive occasions with no identifiable underlying cause of hsCRP elevation, high-intensity statin therapy can be useful to reduce the risk of ASCVD events.

rows.recommendation: In adults without ASCVD, consideration of reproductive risk markers, such as early menopause (<45 years old) and history of adverse pregnancy outcomes (gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm delivery) is reasonable to personalize ASCVD risk assessment when considering the potential benefit of initiating LLT as an adjunct to lifestyle management for primary ASCVD prevention.

In adults at intermediate risk and select adults at borderline risk with no prior ASCVD, if the decision regarding LLT remains uncertain, a CAC score should be used for further risk stratification and to guide the decision to withhold, postpone, or initiate therapy.

In adults at intermediate risk or select adults at borderline risk who undergo CAC testing, if the CAC score is 0 AU and there is preference to avoid LLT and focus on lifestyle management and no higher risk conditions (FH or severe hypercholesterolemia ≥190 mg/dL, diabetes and age >40 years, current cigarette smoking, strong family history of premature ASCVD) are present, it is reasonable to defer therapy and reassess with repeat CAC testing in 3 to 7 years to personalize management.

In adults at intermediate risk and select adults at borderline risk, if the CAC score is >0 AU, it is recommended to initiate LLT, particularly if the CAC score is ≥100 AU or ≥75th standardized percentile to reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults at intermediate or high risk with no prior ASCVD, if there is uncertainty about the intensity of LLT, a CAC score can be useful to refine treatment goals and decide whether to intensify lipid-lowering therapies.

In adults with no prior ASCVD, if incidental CAC is identified on noncardiac CT scans (eg, by visual estimation or a validated artificial intelligence–based algorithm), the presence of coronary atherosclerosis should be considered during decision-making about initiation or intensification of LLT to reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults at low (<3%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD who have an LDL-C <160 mg/dL (4.1 mmol/L) and a 30-year risk estimate of <10% (for those aged 30-59 years), counseling on health behaviors is recommended to reduce LDL-C and risk for ASCVD.

In adults at low (<3%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD but with an LDL-C of 160 to 189 mg/dL (4.1-4.9 mmol/L) or a 30-year ASCVD risk ≥10% (for those aged 30-59 years), a moderate-intensity statin is reasonable to reduce cumulative exposure to atherogenic lipoproteins.

In adults at borderline (3% to <5%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD in whom a decision is made to initiate statin therapy for primary prevention, a moderate-intensity statin is reasonable to achieve ≥30% to 49% LDL-C reduction and to reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults at intermediate (5% to <10%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD, at least a moderate-intensity statin is recommended to achieve ≥30% to 49% LDL-C reduction and to reduce ASCVD risk; for those in the higher end of this risk range, a high-intensity statin is beneficial to further reduce LDL-C by ≥50% and reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults with a CAC score of ≥300 to 999 AU, treatment with LDL-C lowering therapies with consideration of statin therapy as first line is recommended to achieve at least a 50% lowering in LDL-C and a goal of LDL-C <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L).

figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Left panel: Definitions of Class (Strength) of Recommendation:
• Class 1 (Strong): Benefit >>> Risk; suggested phrases: “Is recommended,” “Is indicated/useful/effective/beneficial,” “Should be performed/administered/other,” plus comparative-effectiveness phrases.
• Class 2a (Moderate): Benefit >> Risk; suggested phrases: “Is reasonable,” “Can be useful/effective/beneficial,” plus comparative-effectiveness phrases.
• Class 2b (Weak): Benefit ≥ Risk; suggested phrases: “May/might be reasonable,” “May/might be considered,” “Usefulness/effectiveness is unknown/unclear/uncertain or not well-established.”
• Class 3 No Benefit (Moderate): Benefit = Risk; suggested phrases: “Is not recommended,” “Is not indicated/useful/effective/beneficial,” “Should not be performed/administered/other.”
• Class 3 Harm (Strong): Risk > Benefit; suggested phrases: “Potentially harmful,” “Causes harm,” “Associated with excess morbidity/mortality,” “Should not be performed/administered/other.”
Right panel: Definitions of Level (Quality) of Evidence:
• Level A: High-quality evidence from >1 RCT, meta-analyses of high-quality RCTs, or corroborated by high-quality registry studies.
• Level B-R (Randomized): Moderate-quality evidence from ≥1 RCT, meta-analyses of moderate-quality RCTs.
• Level B-NR (Nonrandomized): Moderate-quality evidence from ≥1 well-designed nonrandomized or registry studies, observational studies, meta-analyses of such studies.
• Level C-LD (Limited Data): Randomized or nonrandomized observational or registry studies with design/execution limitations, meta-analyses, physiological/mechanistic studies in humans.
• Level C-EO (Expert Opinion): Consensus of expert opinion based on clinical experience.

content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis section highlights that abnormal lipid levels affect 20–25% of the population, that apoB-containing lipoproteins are a key cause of ASCVD, and that lipid-lowering therapy reduces risk. Screening asymptomatic individuals can detect multifactorial and monogenic dyslipidemias such as FH before clinical ASCVD develops. Early childhood hypercholesterolemia exposure is linked to subclinical atherosclerosis and higher midlife ASCVD risk, making early lipid screening and treatment both safe and effective. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text details the high prevalence of elevated LDL-C and HeFH in US adults and children, many of whom are unaware of their risk, and reinforces the rationale for universal lipid screening despite limited trial data in younger adults.

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults, screening with a lipid profile is recommended beginning at age 19 years and at least every 5 years thereafter to identify treatable ASCVD risk, with frequent screening recommended for individuals with additional ASCVD risk factors.1,2
2. In children 9 to 11 years of age not previously tested, it is recommended to screen with a lipid profile to identify familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) and other significant lipid disorders.3-6

3. In individuals with first- or second-degree relatives with premature ASCVD, severe hypercholesterolemia, or FH, it is reasonable to perform screening with a single lipid profile (eg, cascade screening) starting at ≥2 years of age to identify FH.7-10

section_headings: 3.2. Measurement of TC, LDL-C, HDL-C, TG, and Non-HDL-C
content.narrative_summary: The page discusses the low rates (10–20%) of lipid screening in the U.S. pediatric population and the inadequacy of family history alone to detect lipid disorders. It highlights feasibility and recommendations for universal childhood screening (ages 9–11 years), catch-up screening, and use of nonfasting TC and HDL-C to calculate non-HDL-C. The HeFH phenotype affects ~1 in 250–300 individuals with elevated ASCVD risk, and cascade (“reverse cascade”) screening of relatives and panel-based genetic testing for pathogenic FH variants are recommended when there is family history of premature ASCVD or primary hypercholesterolemia.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Measurement of TC, LDL-C, HDL-C, TG, and Non-HDL-C. Referenced studies that support recommendations are summarized in the Evidence Table.

rows.recommendation: In adults and children, a standard nonfasting or fasting lipid profile is recommended to document baseline lipid levels, estimate ASCVD risk, and guide initiation of LLT.

In adults and children with a family history of dyslipidemia or premature ASCVD, a personally known or suspected disorder in TG metabolism, or whose nonfasting lipid profile reveals a TG level ≥400 mg/dL (≥4.5 mmol/L), a fasting lipid profile should be performed to more accurately estimate the LDL-C level.

In adults and children who have undergone a standard lipid profile, use of either the Martin/Hopkins equation or the Sampson/National Institutes of Health (NIH) equation is preferred over calculation by the Friedewald equation to estimate LDL-C.

In adults and children who have undergone a standard lipid profile, use of either the Martin/Hopkins equation or Sampson/NIH equation is preferred over direct LDL-C measurement (other than by beta-quantification) to estimate LDL-C.
In adults and children who have undergone a standard lipid profile, reporting of non-HDL-C is recommended for ASCVD risk assessment and to guide initiation and monitoring of LLT.

In adults and children, routine advanced lipoprotein testing (eg, gradient gel electrophoresis, density gradient ultracentrifugation, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, ion mobility analysis) to assess lipoprotein subclasses and parameters such as LDL particle size is not recommended to estimate ASCVD risk and guide initiation of LLT.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Primary Prevention in Adults 30 to 79 Years With LDL-C Levels 70 to 189 mg/dL (1.8-4.9 mmol/L)

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults being assessed for primary prevention of ASCVD, health behavior recommendations should be provided in addition to a benefit-risk discussion for consideration of LLT¹⁻⁴ (Section 4.1.2, “Dietary Approaches in Dyslipidemia”).

2. In adults aged 30 to 59 years, at low (<3%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD who have an LDL-C <160 mg/dL (4.1 mmol/L) and a 30-year risk estimate of <10%, counseling on health behaviors is recommended to reduce LDL-C and risk for ASCVD.¹⁻⁴

3. In adults aged 30 to 59 years, at low (<3%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD but with an LDL-C of 160 to 189 mg/dL (4.1–4.9 mmol/L) or a 30-year ASCVD risk ≥10% (for those aged 30–59 years), a moderate-intensity statin is reasonable to reduce cumulative exposure to atherogenic lipoproteins.

4. In adults at borderline (3% to <5%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD in whom a decision is made to initiate statin therapy for primary prevention, a moderate-intensity statin is reasonable to achieve ≥30% to 49% LDL-C reduction and to reduce ASCVD risk.

5. In adults at intermediate (5% to <10%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD, at least a moderate-intensity statin is recommended to achieve ≥30% to 49% LDL-C reduction and to reduce ASCVD risk; for those in the higher end of this risk range, a high-intensity statin is beneficial to further reduce LDL-C by ≥50% and reduce ASCVD risk.

6. In adults at borderline (3% to <5%) or intermediate (5% to <10%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD in whom statin therapy is initiated, it is reasonable to treat to a goal of LDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <130 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L) to reduce ASCVD risk.

7. In adults at high (≥10%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD in whom LLT is initiated for primary prevention, high-intensity statin therapy is recommended to achieve an LDL-C reduction of ≥50% to reduce the risk of ASCVD.

8. In adults at high (≥10%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD in whom a decision to initiate statin therapy is made, it is reasonable to treat to a goal of LDL-C <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) to reduce ASCVD risk.

It summarizes randomized trials and meta-analyses showing statin therapy benefits across different baseline risk levels, outlines risk thresholds (30-year risk ≥10%, 10-year risk 3%-<5%, 5%-<10%, ≥10%), and recommends moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy to achieve specified LDL-C reductions (≥30% for intermediate risk, ≥50% for high risk) or target LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals. It presents Recommendation 8 on initiating statin therapy in adults at high (≥10%) 10-year ASCVD risk to achieve LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals; Recommendation 9 on intensification of lipid-lowering therapy for those at similar risk; and Recommendation 10 on considering adjunct nonstatin agents such as bempedoic acid, bile acid sequestrants, PCSK9 inhibitors, and inclisiran, with ongoing outcome trials.

rows.recommendation: 8. When initiating statin therapy in adults at high (≥10%) 10-year risk for ASCVD, it is reasonable to treat to an LDL-C goal of <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL based on the likelihood of patient benefit and drug safety and efficacy. An analysis from CARDIA demonstrated that even small increments of LDL-C area under the curve were associated with a significant increase in event rate noted over 20 years, highlighting the potential for early intervention to improve long-term event rates. A systematic review and meta-analysis examining different lipid-lowering interventions showed that the relative risk of MACE was associated with the absolute reduction in LDL-C level, and 5-year rates of major coronary events (coronary death or MI) correlated with achieved LDL-C levels even in individuals being treated for primary prevention.

9. Individuals at high (≥10%) 10-year estimated risk for ASCVD, based on the PREVENT-ASCVD equations, have an event risk that is similar to patients with established ASCVD, warranting intensification of LLT, with the goal of attaining an LDL-C goal of <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L). Meta-analyses of multiple clinical trials show benefit in achieving low, sustained absolute LDL-C levels as well as benefit from ≥50% reduction in LDL-C. Combination therapies with statins and ezetimibe have also been shown to be effective and well tolerated, making it reasonable to consider high-intensity statins or statin combined with ezetimibe to achieve an optimal LDL-C reduction.

10. Beyond ezetimibe, additional agents can be considered as adjuncts to maximally tolerated statins in individuals at high risk for ASCVD. Bempedoic acid has been shown to reduce ASCVD events in high-risk primary prevention populations, demonstrating a significant reduction in MACE compared with placebo. section_headings: 4.2.5. Diabetes in Adults Without Established ASCVD
Recommendations for Adults With Diabetes Without Established ASCVD
content.narrative_summary: Most adults 40 to 75 years of age with diabetes are at intermediate or high risk for a first ASCVD event. Moderate-intensity statin therapy (≥30% to 49% LDL-C reduction) reduces ASCVD risk, while high-intensity statins (≥50% LDL-C reduction) benefit older adults (>50 men, >60 women). Ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, or PCSK9 inhibitors are options for statin-intolerant patients. Adults 20 to 39 are typically low 10-year risk but may warrant therapy if they have long-standing diabetes or other high-risk conditions. ASCVD risk increases over time, and some adults ≥30 may reach intermediate risk by PREVENT-ASCVD equations, guiding treatment per general primary prevention recommendations. Adults >75 with diabetes and ≥2.5-year life expectancy may reasonably initiate moderate-intensity statins after clinician–patient discussion. Icosapent ethyl may reduce residual risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Adults With Diabetes Without Established ASCVD

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults 40 to 75 years of age with diabetes and without clinical ASCVD, moderate-intensity statin therapy is indicated to achieve a ≥30% to 49% reduction in LDL-C and a goal of LDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <130 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L) to reduce ASCVD risk.
2. In adults with diabetes who have statin-attributed side effects, initiation of ezetimibe and/or bempedoic acid or a PCSK9 mAb is recommended to lower LDL-C and reduce ASCVD risk.

3. In adults 40 to 75 years of age with diabetes who have multiple ASCVD risk factors, it is reasonable to prescribe high-intensity statin therapy to achieve a ≥50% reduction in LDL-C and a goal of LDL-C <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) to reduce ASCVD risk.

4. In adults with diabetes without ASCVD but with additional ASCVD risk factor(s)* on a statin with an LDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) and elevated fasting TG (150-499 mg/dL [1.7–5.6 mmol/L]), the addition of IPE may be considered to reduce ASCVD risk.
rows.supporting_text: *As per REDUCE-IT inclusion criteria, high-risk features include men ≥55 years or women ≥65 years, cigarette smoking or stopped smoking within 3 months; hypertension (blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg or on antihypertensive medication); HDL-C ≤40 mg/dL for men or ≤50 mg/dL for women; high-sensitivity C-reactive protein >3.0 mg/L (if measured); renal dysfunction; retinopathy; albuminuria; ankle-brachial index <0.9 without symptoms of intermittent claudication.

rows.recommendation: 5. In adults with diabetes and 10-year ASCVD risk of ≥10% by the PREVENT-ASCVD equations, it may be reasonable to add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 mAb to maximally tolerated statin therapy to achieve an LDL-C goal of <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) to reduce ASCVD risk.

6. In adults >75 years of age with diabetes and an estimated life expectancy of at least 2.5 years, it may be reasonable to initiate moderate-intensity statin therapy after a clinician–patient discussion of potential benefits and risks to reduce ASCVD risk.

7. In adults 20 to 39 years of age with diabetes of long duration (≥10 years of type 2 diabetes, ≥20 years of type 1 diabetes), albuminuria (≥30 μg of albumin/mg creatinine), eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2, retinopathy, neuropathy, or ankle-brachial index <0.9, it may be reasonable to initiate moderate-intensity statin therapy to reduce ASCVD risk.

content.narrative_summary: This page provides supportive evidence for lipid-lowering therapy in adults aged 40–75 years with diabetes for primary prevention of ASCVD. It summarizes data from multiple RCTs showing that moderate-intensity statin therapy reduces ASCVD risk by approximately 25%–30%, with similar benefits in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The CLEAR Outcomes trial demonstrated a 13% RRR in MACE with bempedoic acid in statin-intolerant patients. Ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors (alirocumab, evolocumab) further lower LDL-C and MACE risk. The PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations are recommended to identify patients who may benefit from high-intensity therapy. The REDUCE-IT trial showed a 25% RRR in MACE with 4 g/day EPA in patients with elevated triglycerides, although bleeding risks were noted.

Clinical ASCVD at Very High Risk

content.narrative_summary: Statin therapy is the foundation of lipid‐lowering treatment for secondary prevention, given its proven efficacy, safety, tolerability, ease, and cost‐effectiveness.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Secondary ASCVD Prevention

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with clinical ASCVD who are not at very high risk (Figure 10), high‐intensity statin therapy should be initiated to achieve a ≥50% reduction in LDL‐C and a goal of LDL‐C <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <100 mg/dL to reduce the risk of recurrent ASCVD events.

2. In adults with clinical ASCVD who are not at very high risk and on maximally tolerated statin therapy, it is reasonable to add ezetimibe, a PCSK9 mAb, or bempedoic acid (selection depending on degree of LDL‐C lowering needed and patient preference) to achieve a goal of LDL‐C <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <100 mg/dL to reduce the risk of ASCVD events.

3. In adults with clinical ASCVD who are not at very high risk and on maximally tolerated statin therapy, it is reasonable to add ezetimibe, a PCSK9 mAb, or bempedoic acid (selection based on the degree of LDL‐C lowering needed and patient preference) to achieve a goal LDL‐C <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L) and to reduce the risk of ASCVD events.

4. In adults with clinical ASCVD* who are at very high risk (Figure 10 and Figure 11), high‐intensity statin therapy should be initiated to achieve a ≥50% reduction in LDL‐C and a goal LDL‐C <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L) and to reduce the risk of ASCVD events.

5. In adults with clinical ASCVD who are at very high risk and on maximally tolerated statin therapy, ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 mAb should be added (selected based on the degree of LDL‐C lowering needed and patient preference) to achieve a goal of LDL‐C <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L) to reduce risk of ASCVD events.

6. In adults with clinical ASCVD who are at very high risk on maximally tolerated statin therapy, it is reasonable to add bempedoic acid, with or without ezetimibe and/or PCSK9 mAb, to reach an LDL‐C goal <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L) to reduce the risk of ASCVD events.

7. In adults with clinical ASCVD who are at very high risk and on maximally tolerated statin therapy with or without ezetimibe, it is reasonable to add inclisiran† in those unable to tolerate or obtain evolocumab or alirocumab or have a strong preference for less frequent dosing to achieve an LDL‐C goal <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and non‐HDL‐C <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L).

8. In adults with HFrEF attributable to ischemic heart disease who have a reasonable life expectancy (3-5 years) and are not already on a statin because of ASCVD, it may be reasonable to consider initiation of moderate‐intensity statin therapy to reduce the occurrence of ASCVD events.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative describes the graded association between LDL-C lowering and ASCVD risk reduction, highlighting evidence from RCTs that combination therapies (e.g., adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 mAb) yield greater risk reduction than statin monotherapy. It notes expanded safety data for PCSK9 mAbs, reduced cost, and that newer nonstatin therapies (bempedoic acid, inclisiran) also lower LDL-C, though long-term outcome trials are ongoing. It references Figures 10 and 12 and reports no safety signals at very low LDL-C levels.

content.narrative_summary: This section discusses the benefits of high-intensity statin therapy in lowering LDL-C by ≥50% and reducing ASCVD events. It reviews results from CVOTs supporting high-intensity statins as a Class 1 indication and notes that moderate-dose statins with nonstatins may optimize LDL lowering. The IMPROVE-IT trial showed a trend toward benefit with ezetimibe added to simvastatin, and multiple nonstatin therapies (ezetimibe, evolocumab, alirocumab, bempedoic acid) have favorable safety profiles and can be added in adults with ASCVD who cannot achieve LDL-C <70 mg/dL on statin alone. It is reasonable to treat non-very-high-risk ASCVD patients to LDL-C <55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL. Meta-analyses and RCTs demonstrate continuous ASCVD risk reduction with lower LDL-C, including additional benefits when baseline LDL-C is already low. FOURIER, ODYSSEY, and FOURIER-OLE trials of PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies demonstrated further ASCVD event reduction and acceptable safety.

content.title: 4.2.8.3. Older Adults
content.narrative_summary: As adults age, decision-making about lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) should balance the goals of ASCVD prevention against medication-related harms, considering functional status, multimorbidity, frailty, polypharmacy, and life expectancy rather than chronological age alone. Data on primary prevention in adults >75 years are limited; ongoing trials aim to clarify benefits in those ≥70 years. Coronary artery calcium scoring may help reclassify low-CAC older adults to avoid LLT when life expectancy and patient priorities favor de-escalation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Older Adults. Referenced studies that support recommendations are summarized in the Evidence Table.

rows.recommendation: 1. In older adults, the benefit–risk discussion should include patient priorities, functional status, multimorbidity, frailty, polypharmacy, and life expectancy, and should not be based solely on chronological age when considering the decision to discontinue LLT.

2. In adults aged >75 years with an estimated life expectancy of at least 2.5 years, it may be reasonable to initiate moderate-intensity statin therapy after a clinician–patient discussion of potential benefits and risks to reduce ASCVD risk.
3. In patients with a life expectancy of <1 year, it may be reasonable to discontinue LDL-lowering therapy to avoid unnecessary medication use or adverse medication effects.

4. In adults aged >75 years with an estimated life expectancy of at least 2.5 years, and for whom the decision regarding LLT is uncertain, it may be reasonable to measure CAC to reclassify those with minimal (1–10) or no CAC to avoid LLT.

5. In pregnant individuals with FH or a history of clinical ASCVD, it may be reasonable to continue statin therapy to lower LDL-C and ASCVD risk following an individualized benefit-risk discussion.9

section_headings: Recommendations for Adults With CKD—Stage 3 or Higher
content.narrative_summary: Adults with chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease, spondyloarthritis) have higher ASCVD risk that may be underestimated by standard calculators; clinicians should incorporate CID-specific risk factors into decision making and monitor lipids, especially when on anti-inflammatory therapy. CKD stage 3 or higher is a risk factor for ASCVD; in these patients, statin therapy (moderate-intensity for primary prevention and high-intensity for those with ASCVD), often combined with ezetimibe or PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, is recommended to achieve target LDL-C reductions. For patients on maintenance hemodialysis, continuation of statin therapy may be reasonable, individualized by survival, comorbidities, and ASCVD severity.

rows.recommendation: In adults 40 to 75 years of age with CKD stage 3 or higher and an LDL-C of 70 to 189 mg/dL (1.8-4.9 mmol/L), moderate-intensity statin therapy or moderate-intensity statin combined with ezetimibe is recommended to reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults with CKD stage 3 or higher and clinical ASCVD, LLT with high-intensity statin therapy, with or without ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 mAb, is recommended to achieve a ≥50% reduction in LDL-C levels and a goal of LDL-C <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L) to reduce ASCVD risk.

In adults with CKD who require maintenance hemodialysis, it may be reasonable to continue statin therapy to reduce the risk of ASCVD events. Treatment decisions should be individualized with consideration of expected survival, other comorbidities, and severity of ASCVD.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis notes that observational and genetic epidemiology demonstrate a strong association between triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnants and ASCVD risk. Persistent hypertriglyceridemia (fasting TG ≥150 mg/dL) after evaluation of secondary causes requires 4 to 12 weeks of lifestyle management and statin therapy based on ASCVD risk. Cardiovascular risk is highest with TG levels of 500–880 mg/dL, and the risk of pancreatitis increases above 500 mg/dL, particularly at levels ≥1000 mg/dL, where pharmacotherapy decisions should consider clinical ASCVD, diabetes, patient age, and calculated ASCVD risk. Lifestyle management is first-line, including diet low in saturated fats and refined carbohydrates, alcohol reduction, weight loss, and exercise, which reduce TG levels. For patients with clinical ASCVD and persistent hypertriglyceridemia, LDL-C lowering remains the priority, with nonstatin therapies reducing residual risk. Familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS) is described as a monogenic disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the gene encoding lipoprotein lipase, resulting in severely elevated TG levels.

content.narrative_summary: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a largely genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), with levels ≥50 mg/dL (~125 nmol/L) conferring ~40% higher relative risk and higher levels associated with progressively greater risk. Lifestyle interventions and statins have minimal impact on Lp(a), whereas PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies and lipoprotein apheresis lower both Lp(a) and LDL-C; apheresis is FDA-approved for patients with Lp(a) ≥60 mg/dL who also have familial hypercholesterolemia and CAD or PAD.
